narrative: The model estimated a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a slightly-more-likely-than-not estimate, not a certainty, but it was high enough that the admissions decision treated it as a meaningful risk and denied your application. The strongest factor was your LSAT score: 20, compared with an average of about 37 among accepted students. Because this was the top influence and it pushed the prediction toward failure, it carried substantial weight. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 was the second most influential factor. It is only slightly below the accepted-student average of 3.23, but importantly it pushed in the opposite direction—toward passing—and therefore worked somewhat in your favor. The third factor was your first-year academic decile, which was 1 versus an average of 6 for accepted students; this also pushed toward failure. To strengthen a future application, focus first on raising your LSAT through structured preparation and, if feasible, a retake. Seek advising on how to present your academic trajectory, especially the early-year standing, and consider programs or schools that review applications holistically or offer conditional admission. Ask admissions staff what evidence they would need to reconsider, and build a clear plan showing improved test performance and academic readiness.
